title: What are Flink windows (tumbling / sliding / session / global, count-based vs time-based) and their components (assigner, trigger, evictor), and what is a watermark (a logical event-time marker, watermark = max_event_ts − max_out_of_order_delay, e.g. forBoundedOutOfOrderness) used to trigger windows and handle out-of-order/late events?
shortTitle: What are Flink windows and watermarks

s1_definition.oneliner: A Flink window slices the endless stream into finite buckets for aggregation, and a watermark is the clock that tells each bucket when it is safe to close and emit its result.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Window** – Groups an unbounded stream of events into finite buckets so that an aggregation function can run over each bucket.
- **Tumbling window** – Fixed-size, non-overlapping; each event belongs to exactly one window.
- **Sliding window** – Fixed-size, overlapping by a slide interval; one event can belong to multiple windows.
- **Session window** – Gap-based; closes after a period of inactivity, merging events into bursts.
- **Global window** – One window for all events; fires only when a custom trigger decides.
- **Watermark** – A special marker flowing with the stream asserting that event time has progressed to a certain point, computed as max-event-time minus out-of-orderness tolerance.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants to count how many transactions Rajesh makes every one minute. A tumbling window divides the day into back-to-back one-minute slots. A sliding window is like a security guard who every ten seconds looks back over the last minute. A session window groups a shopping session and closes when Rajesh goes quiet for five minutes. The watermark is the bank manager announcing "it is now safely 10:01, close the 10:00-to-10:01 slot and publish the count."

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Flink Window Types

  Tumbling (1 min):
  |-------|-------|-------|-------|
  | W1    | W2    | W3    | W4    |
  Each event in exactly one window

  Sliding (1 min size, 10s slide):
  |-------|       |-------|
    |-------|       |-------|
      |-------|       |-------|
  Events can be in multiple windows

  Session (5 min gap):
  |--events--|     5min gap     |--events--|
  |  Session 1  |               | Session 2 |
  Closes after inactivity gap

  Watermark driving window firing:
  Events: ──T1──T2──T3──T4──T5──▶
  Max ts: ─02──05──03──08──10──▶
  WM(-5s): ─57──00──00──03──05──▶
                 ▲         ▲
          W[10:00,10:01)  W[10:00,10:01)
          NOT yet fired   fires at WM=10:01
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Flink window turns an endless, unbounded stream into finite buckets that an aggregation can run over. There are four shapes: tumbling windows chop time into fixed, non-overlapping slots; sliding windows provide overlapping views that advance by a smaller slide; session windows group bursts of activity and close after a gap of inactivity; and global windows put everything into one window and rely on a custom trigger.

The piece that makes event-time windows correct is the watermark. Streams arrive out of order because of network delays and retries, so Flink needs a principled way to say "I have probably now seen everything up to time T." A watermark is exactly that assertion. The common strategy is bounded out of orderness, where the watermark is the maximum event time seen minus a tolerance. When the watermark crosses a window's end, the trigger fires that window.

Events that arrive after the watermark has passed their window are late. By default Flink drops them, but you can keep the window open with allowed lateness or route late events to a side output for separate handling. The out-of-orderness tolerance trades latency against completeness: a larger value waits longer and captures more stragglers but adds delay.

At the National Bank of India Rajesh used one-minute tumbling event-time windows to count transactions per account per minute for fraud detection, with a five-second watermark to absorb normal mobile-network delays. Genuinely late events were routed to a quarantine side output rather than dropped silently, because in banking you cannot lose a transaction.

Remember one sentence: A window slices the stream into finite buckets, and the watermark is the clock that tells each bucket when it is safe to close, fire, and emit its result.

---

keyPoints: Tumbling windows are fixed-size and non-overlapping; each event belongs to exactly one window.
Sliding windows overlap by a slide interval, giving more frequent views at the cost of duplicate processing per event.
Session windows close after a configurable gap of inactivity, grouping bursts of activity dynamically.
A watermark is computed as max-event-time minus out-of-orderness tolerance and drives window firing.
Late events arriving after the watermark has passed their window are dropped by default, but allowed lateness and side outputs can capture them.
Every window has three components: the assigner (routes events to windows), the trigger (decides when to fire), and the optional evictor (prunes elements).
